Just last offseason, the Blue Jays signed pitcher Dylan Cease to the biggest pitching contract of the hot stove season. They likely won't come close to that again with Skubal off the board, but Peralta would add another upgrade to the starting rotation.

Peralta could slide into the Blue Jays rotation as their No. 2 starter behind Cease and complete the group alongside Trey Yesavage, Jose Soriano and Cody Ponce.

The San Diego Padres, Chicago White Sox, Chicago Cubs and Rays are also reportedly interested in Peralta.

articles.title: Tarik Skubal Hyped by Mets' Steve Cohen After Historic $450M Contract in MLB Free Agency
articles.summary: Tarik Skubal made quite the impression on the New York Mets before signing the most lucrative contract in baseball history.
articles.body:
Tarik Skubal made quite the impression on the New York Mets before signing the most lucrative contract in baseball history.

The team brass left their meeting with Skubal "blown away," The Athletic's Will Sammon reported on Sunday.

"He impressed Mets officials with his discipline when the pitcher detailed his workouts," Sammon wrote. "When he spoke about the Mets, he didn't just tick off the obvious components of the roster; Skubal rattled off names of pitchers in the farm system."

Mets owner Steve Cohen seemed particularly impressed.

"I don't have to worry about him pitching in New York," Cohen said, per the New York Post 's Jon Heyman . "He's an outstanding individual."

The 30-year-old met the team last week in California and took over the session without relying on agent Scott Boras, according to Sammon.

Skubal reportedly discussed everything from his family priorities to his desire to win, and he impressed the Mets executives with the intricacies of his workout regimen.

Mets owner Steve Cohen and president of baseball operations David Stearns entered the meeting "with a certain number in mind," according to Sammon. They were so impressed by Skubal that they were "comfortable with increasing" that figure by the end of the meeting.

Ultimately, that resulted in a nine-year, $450 million contract, surpassing Los Angeles Dodgers pitcher Yoshinobu Yamamoto's 12-year, $325 million contract. Skubal's average annual salary of $50 million nearly doubled Yamamoto's $27.1 million annual figure.

Stearns has not issued a contract to a pitcher longer than three years during his tenure with the team. The Mets "sometimes avoid long-term arrangements with other players so they can be in the mix for players like Skubal," according to Sammon.

Before signing Skubal, they trailed only the Los Angeles Dodgers and New York Yankees in total payroll allocations .

Despite their expensive roster, the Mets have proven that championships cannot simply be bought. They finished the 2026 season in last place in the National League East with a 74-88 record, but that clearly hasn't stopped New York from continuing to believe in their top-heavy approach to roster building. With Skubal, Juan Soto, Bo Bichette and Francisco Lindor, the Mets now have $1.68 billion invested in just four players.

articles.title: Every MLB Team's Biggest Free-Agent Signing Ever After Tarik Skubal's $450M Mets Contract
articles.summary: The Tarik Skubal chase appears to be over, with the New York Mets reportedly agreeing to a nine-year, $450 million contract, pending a physical. It would be the largest-ever deal for a full-time pitcher and one of the biggest ever for a free agent of any kind.
articles.body:
The Tarik Skubal chase appears to be over, with the New York Mets reportedly agreeing to a nine-year, $450 million contract, pending a physical. It would be the largest-ever deal for a full-time pitcher and one of the biggest ever for a free agent of any kind.

So now seems as good a time as any to look back at the biggest free-agent signing in each MLB team's history.

This is generally a modern list, as every signing in here has taken place in the last 20 years. Yet it contains multitudes, with contracts ranging everywhere from just $39 million all the way up to $765 million.

We'll go division by division, starting in the American League East and ending in the National League West.

Baltimore Orioles: Chris Davis for 7 years, $161 million in 2016

Sorry for bringing this one up, Orioles fans. It always was a specious contract, as Davis wasn't going to have much to fall back on if he lost any of the power that propelled him to MLB home run titles in 2013 and 2015. Even so, it was hard to see him devolving into a historically bad hitter (-5.8 rWAR between 2017 and 2020) who would have to take an early retirement .

Boston Red Sox: David Price for 7 years, $217 million in 2015

Price was a five-time All-Star and Cy Young Award winner when he arrived in Boston and, alas, he didn't add any more to either pile. Yet he was at least a solidly above-average pitcher (118 ERA+) with the Red Sox, and Boston fans haven't forgotten that he was the tip of the spear for the club's last World Series championship in 2018.

New York Yankees: Aaron Judge for 9 years, $360 million in 2022

As Judge was fresh off a 62-homer season yet also already 30, there was a sense that the Yankees might have bought high with this contract. Yet if you'd told them he would win two more MVPs in the first four years of the deal, they would have taken it. No matter what happens over the remainder of the contract, Judge has arguably already justified it with those first four seasons.

Tampa Bay Rays: Zach Eflin for 3 years, $40 million in 2022

Eflin was coming off an injury-shortened season when this deal went down, so it seemed a rather odd way for the Rays to flex their limited financial muscle. Yet even if he was traded as soon as 2024, at least Tampa Bay got his best season first. In 2023, he led the AL with 16 wins and posted a personal-best (by far) 3.6 rWAR.

Toronto Blue Jays: Dylan Cease for 7 years, $210 million in 2025

Just in case anyone missed the nuance, this is about free-agent signings. Vladimir Guerrero Jr.'s 14-year, $500 million deal was a contract extension.

For Cease's part, it's hard to do better for a debut in a new city than a season that results in a runner-up finish in the AL Cy Young Award voting. Now the question is if he can level out what has been a pattern of up-and-down returns to this point in his major league career.

Chicago White Sox: Andrew Benintendi for 5 years, $75 million in 2022

Front offices have gotten pretty smart over the last couple decades, to a point where it's rare to behold a proper "What are they thinking?!" signing. This was one of those. A club-record contract for a singles hitter? It's gone about as well (i.e., 0.5 rWAR total ) as anyone expected, though Benintendi has at least had the courtesy to turn on the power in the last few seasons.

Cleveland Guardians: Edwin Encarnacion for 3 years, $60 million in 2016

The fact that this is Cleveland's high mark in free agency says a lot about the franchise, but it was a well-timed risk that aged just fine. They were fresh off going to the World Series when they inked Encarnacion, and he ended up averaging 35 home runs throughout the life of the contract. He had averaged 39 home runs in the five seasons prior.

Detroit Tigers: Prince Fielder for 9 years, $214 million in 2012

This one might not have happened if Victor Martinez hadn't torn his ACL in January of 2012. It never figured to age well, and Fielder's production indeed started going south well before he called it a career in 2016. The final return on this contract was just 6.8 rWAR. But hey, at least the Tigers escaped the deal early and somehow landed Ian Kinsler in a 2013 trade with the Texas Rangers.

Kansas City Royals: Alex Gordon for 4 years, $72 million in 2016

This was an emotional signing, not a logical one. As much as Gordon still meant to the Royals when he helped them win the World Series in 2015, that year also sure looked like the start of his post-prime years. And it was. He managed just 3.8 rWAR during the life of this contract, a far cry from the 5.9 rWAR he had averaged between 2011 and 2014.

Minnesota Twins: Carlos Correa for 6 years, $200 million in 2023

This was Correa's second deal with the Twins, and it had felt like a "neener neener" in the direction of the San Francisco Giants and New York Mets . Correa was sitting pretty after posting 5.3 rWAR in 2022 and then using his opt-out, only for agreements with both clubs to fall apart over concerns about his physical. Alas, he has since missed about half of all possible games and has become something of a forgotten man following his salary-dump trade back to the Houston Astros in 2025.

Athletics: Luis Severino for 3 years, $67 million in 2024

The A's committed $67 million to Severino in December 2024 as increased revenue-sharing payments added pressure to boost their payroll. The actual fit was baffling from the start, and the return thus far includes a 98 ERA+, a 2.5 rWAR and a shoulder injury that cost him much of 2026. He has a 5.85 ERA when pitching in Sacramento, where he's no fan of Sutter Health Park . So, things are going great.

Houston Astros: Carlos Lee for 6 years, $100 million in 2006

This is the only contract in here that's almost old enough to buy a drink. Yet even if the notion of a power-only hitter getting nine figures is laughable by today's standards, this really could have gone worse for Houston. Lee hit 110 home runs in his first four seasons in Houston, and his final 117 OPS+ as an Astro is actually higher than his career mark of 113.

Los Angeles Angels: Anthony Rendon for 7 years, $245 million in 2019

Rendon's 2020 debut as an Angel went swimmingly, even if the pandemic-shortened season limited him to 52 games. The Angels then got just 205 games and 1.7 rWAR from him through 2024, and he missed the entire 2025 season following hip surgery. Off the field, former Angels All-Star Mark Trumbo criticized his reluctance to speak with reporters. Rendon also served a four-game suspension following a 2023 confrontation in which video showed him grabbing a fan's shirt; police investigated but filed no charges. The contract was a gold-medal contender at the Bad Contract Olympics.

Seattle Mariners: Robinson Canó for 10 years, $240 million in 2013

It was a heck of a thing to behold the Mariners, of all teams, outbidding the Yankees to land Canó in free agency 13 years ago. And even if he went on to sully his reputation with two suspensions under MLB's drug policy, the story of his contract consists of the Mariners getting 23.9 rWAR in five seasons and then trading away the remaining five years, albeit with cash and Edwin Díaz included in the deal. Even if Jarred Kelenic didn't pan out, Seattle still avoided the contract's worst years.

Texas Rangers: Corey Seager for 10 years, $325 million in 2021

The buzz of the moment suggests that this partnership could be close to ending . If so, well, may it end on good terms. Seager has a 140 OPS+ and 25.4 rWAR as a Ranger, not to mention a World Series ring from a 2023 run in which he was a central hero . As it stands, this is one of the better free-agent signings in recent memory, if not all-time.

The 25 Biggest Contracts in Sports History 💰

Atlanta Braves: B.J. Upton for 5 years, $75.25 million in 2012

An average season for Upton before this deal consisted of 20-plus home runs and 30-plus stolen bases, so the bet on the talent made some sense. But he was also coming off a .298 OBP, so his subsequent tumble into an erratic, replacement-level player wasn't a total shock. No wonder the Braves have largely avoided the high end of the free agent market ever since.

Miami Marlins: José Reyes for 6 years, $106 million in 2011

This was the signing that was meant to announce the Marlins as a power player in the NL East. They certainly bought high on Reyes, who was coming off winning the NL batting title and leading MLB in triples for a fourth time. But he was never the same player afterward, and the Marlins pulled the plug after one year. The story is pretty much Jeffrey Loria's ownership in one neat little nutshell.

New York Mets: Juan Soto for 15 years, $765 million in 2024

Soto's first two seasons as a Met haven't exactly ushered in a new era, but that's hardly his fault. He finished third in the NL MVP voting in 2025 and had a .908 OPS in a "down" 2026 season. He'll be fine. And given how deep Steve Cohen's pockets go, any failure to win during Soto's tenure won't be because they spent too much on him. Or at least, one would hope.

As for Skubal, the largest ever contract for a free-agent pitcher before him belonged to Yoshinobu Yamamoto at 12 years and $325 million. Skubal cleared that by $125 million. Yet a better way to look at Skubal's new deal is as the next coming of Gerrit Cole's nine-year, $324 million pact with the New York Yankees. Adjusted for inflation, that deal would be worth $428 million in 2026 dollars.

Either way, Skubal's new contract is essentially a Rorschach test. Maybe you think it's perfect for a two-time Cy Young Award winner who has a 171 ERA+ and 0.923 WHIP for the last three seasons. Or, maybe you think it's too big of a risk for a 30-year-old who's already had multiple elbow surgeries.

Philadelphia Phillies: Bryce Harper for 13 years, $330 million in 2019

As of this year, Harper has been a Phillie for longer than he was a National. Hard to believe, right? Yet he owns an MVP with both franchises, and shockingly similar numbers that include a 143 OPS+ as a Phillie and a 139 OPS+ as a National. He's also showing no signs that he's going to stop hitting any time soon, so this contract has essentially bought a Phillies hat on his Hall of Fame plaque.

Washington Nationals: Stephen Strasburg for 7 years, $245 million in 2019

This is the ultimate cautionary tale of what can happen when a team does a contract with its heart and not its head. Strasburg had been a hero for the Nationals' first World Series-winning team in 2019, but he was also past 30 and had a history of injuries. Even if nobody saw just eight more starts coming, some sort of disaster was never un likely.

Chicago Cubs: Jason Heyward for 8 years, $184 million in 2015

The Cubs signed Heyward when he was coming off a 7.0-rWAR season for the Cardinals. For Chicago, he was worth only 9.1 rWAR in seven seasons before he was granted his release. But at least the Cubs got two Gold Gloves from him. And who knows? Maybe they don't come back and win the 2016 World Series without his rain delay speech .

Cincinnati Reds: Mike Moustakas and Nick Castellanos for 4 years, $64 million apiece in 2019 and 2020, respectively

These deals were signed just weeks apart, and the final return on investment for the Reds was just 1.3 rWAR in total. That includes 3.1 rWAR from Castellanos in 2021, after which he opted out and departed for greener pastures in Philadelphia. So if the Reds could do these deals again—as there's a drive into deep left field by Castellanos and that'll be a home run—they almost certainly would not.

Milwaukee Brewers: Lorenzo Cain for 5 years, $80 million in 2018

This one went down the same day the Brewers traded for Christian Yelich, and the two of them ended up contributing 14.1 rWAR to a squad that made it to the NLCS. That was the high point of Cain's tenure in Milwaukee, but he at least contributed a couple more 2-rWAR seasons before reaching the end of the line in 2022. For an $80 million contract, he was hardly a bust.

Pittsburgh Pirates: Francisco Liriano for 3 years, $39 million in 2014

In a May 2025 USA Today column, Bob Nightengale reported:

"The Pittsburgh Pirates, according to information received by the players union and confirmed by several owners, are one of the most profitable teams in all of baseball, stashing a huge chunk of their revenue sharing monies instead of investing in their team year after year."

Whatever the club's profitability, the fact that Liriano's contract still represents the Pirates' high-water mark in free agency under Bob Nutting is an indictment of their spending ambitions.

St. Louis Cardinals: Matt Holliday for 7 years, $120 million in 2010

This contract paid for four All-Star seasons, plus a World Series ring in 2011 and a National League pennant in 2013. And among hitters who have taken at least 3,000 plate appearances in a Cardinals uniform, Holliday's career 138 OPS+ ranks eighth. It's awfully hard to do better than that when investing in a star. The Cardinals should try it again sometime.

Arizona Diamondbacks: Corbin Burnes for 6 years, $210 million in 2024

An adjustment for inflation would put Zack Greinke's six-year, $206.5 million contract from 2015 in this spot, but we're not getting that eggheaded. In any case, Burnes needed Tommy John surgery just 11 starts into his D-backs career and only just returned this September. The 2021 NL Cy Young Award winner chose not to opt out in October, and it suffices to say that was the wise choice.

Colorado Rockies: Kris Bryant for 7 years, $182 million in 2022

Save for somewhere in the Rockies' front office, there was not a soul on earth who thought this was a good idea. And now, here they stand in the wreckage of just 170 games and -1.6 rWAR to show for Bryant's contract. He was nowhere to be seen in 2026, and is now being treated as something akin to the phantom of Coors Field. The worst free-agent contract of all time? It has a strong case.

Los Angeles Dodgers: Shohei Ohtani for 10 years, $700 million in 2023

Because of his deferrals, Ohtani's contract actually works out to a present-day value in the $460 million range . But come on, we all dig the bigger number. And the Dodgers certainly dig what Ohtani has been for them so far. He was 2-for-2 in winning MVPs and World Series in 2024 and 2025. And even after he fell apart physically this year, he was still the runner-up for the NL MVP.

San Diego Padres: Manny Machado for 10 years, $300 million in 2019

Again, we're talking about free-agent contracts, not extensions. Machado's current 11-year, $350 million deal doesn't count. Either way, the partnership between him and the Padres has been undeniably fruitful. In eight seasons, he's been an All-Star three times and has hit 224 home runs. Before his arrival, the franchise had played in 34 playoff games. Since his arrival, that number has doubled to 68.

San Francisco Giants: Willy Adames for 7 years, $182 million in 2024

Adames' Giants debut ended up being a success story, as he played in 160 games and became the franchise's first 30-homer slugger since Barry Bonds. But then came just 1.7 rWAR this year, and you can tell from the trade rumors that the Giants have some level of understanding that there's no reverse on this engine.

Stats courtesy of Baseball Reference , FanGraphs and Baseball Savant .

articles.title: 6 Cost-Cutting MLB Trade Ideas if a Salary Cap is Implemented
articles.summary: Major League Baseball appears headed for a lockout as the current Collective Bargaining Agreement expires and the owners and players' union remain miles apart on negotiations.
articles.body:
Major League Baseball appears headed for a lockout as the current Collective Bargaining Agreement expires and the owners and players' union remain miles apart on negotiations.

One of the central talking points of the next CBA is the potential implementation of a salary cap and salary floor, and that could force some teams with bloated payrolls to find a way to immediately cut costs.

Ahead we've proposed six cost-cutting trades for teams that rank among the biggest payrolls in baseball, with shedding salary the motivating factor in each of the moves. For the sake of discussion, assumptions were made with regard to a player's willingness to waive his no-trade clause in multiple instances.

These trades might not make obvious sense in a traditional offseason, but could become necessary if a salary cap becomes part of the payroll equation.

The Pirates acquired Brandon Lowe to be the high-priced veteran anchor in a young lineup in 2026, and he responded with a 121 OPS+ and 35 home runs before declining a qualifying offer at the start of the offseason.

Matt Chapman could fill a similar role on the roster and in the middle of the lineup, plugging in as the everyday third baseman and allowing Nick Gonzales to shift back to second base where he is a better fit defensively.

The five-time Gold Glove winner has four years remaining on his contract at roughly $25 million per year, and flipping Mitch Keller would offset a significant chunk of that money in 2027 and 2028 while still representing a sizable salary dump for San Francisco on the back end.

Keller logged a 5.29 ERA in 115.2 innings in 2026, but his 4.54 FIP suggests he was the victim of some bad luck, and a change of scenery could help him take a step back toward All-Star form.

The Pirates get a power bat and a veteran presence, while the Giants add an experienced arm with some upside to slot in behind Logan Webb and clear Chapman from the books for 2029 and 2030.

To BAL: RHP Corbin Burnes, $30 million To ARI: 1B/3B Christian Encarnacion-Strand, LHP Caden Hunter, OF Tyler O'Neill

Corbin Burnes still has four years remaining on his six-year, $210 million contract, and he has made just 14 starts and recorded 74.2 innings of work in his first two seasons with the D-backs.

The 2021 NL Cy Young winner returned from Tommy John surgery in September and shook off the rust with three starts down the stretch, putting him on track to be a full participant heading into the 2027 season.

There's obvious risk given his recent injury issues, but Burnes was still pitching like a frontline starter pre-injury with a 2.66 ERA in 64.1 innings to begin his Arizona tenure in 2025.

The Orioles get a chance to bring back a familiar face, as Burnes served as their ace in 2024 when he finished fifth in AL Cy Young balloting, while also offloading Tyler O'Neill's remaining contract. The $30 million cash inclusion would apply to 2028-30, when O'Neill is no longer offsetting the financial side of the deal.

The D-backs get salary relief, a low-cost controllable option to fill the void at first base in Christian Encarnacion-Strand (213 PA, 134 OPS+, 11 HR) and a standout pitching prospect in Caden Hunter who would plug directly into their Top 10 prospect list.

To ATL: SS Trevor Story, RHP John Holobetz To BOS: IF Brett Wisely

With Franklin Arias breaking down the door following a huge season in the upper levels of the minors, Trevor Story's days as the Red Sox's starting shortstop are numbered.

The two-time All-Star enjoyed a strong bounce-back season in 2025, posting a 104 OPS+ with 25 home runs and 31 steals in a 4.1-WAR campaign, but he again spent much of the year on the sidelines in 2026 with a 75 OPS+ over 64 games.

The Red Sox owe him $25 million in 2027, plus a $5 million buyout on a 2028 club option, and packaging him with a legitimate prospect might be the best way to offload his salary and clear a path for Arias.

Right-hander John Holobetz had a 4.07 ERA and 132 strikeouts in 119.1 innings between Double-A and Triple-A last year, and he would give Atlanta immediate MLB-ready depth.

Brett Wisely is fringe roster depth and could be designated for assignment on the other side of the trade, so this amounts to the Braves absorbing Story's contract as a flier to fill their shortstop need while essentially buying a quality prospect.

To HOU: OF Kevin Alcántara, OF Kane Kepley, RHP Phil Maton

A gutted starting rotation is a major offseason storyline for the Cubs, but they also need to rebuild their relief corps around Daniel Palencia, Ryan Zeferjahn and Jacob Webb.

If the Astros decide to start slashing salary, or even just retooling the roster at something of a crossroads for the organization, Josh Hader and his $19 million salary for 2027 and 2028 would be an obvious place to start.

With a 1.01 ERA, 0.76 WHIP and 11.1 K/9 while recording 26 saves in 45 appearances, Hader has shown no signs of slowing down as he enters his age-33 season.

The cost for late-inning bullpen arms has steadily climbed in recent years, to the point that a $19 million AAV over the next two years for Hader actually represents a team-friendly salary for a club not looking to shed payroll.

That means the Cubs will need to part with some real value. Kevin Alcántara could compete for an outfield job in 2027, Kane Kepley would immediately become a top five prospect in the Houston system and Phil Maton helps offset some short-term money with a $6 million salary for the coming season and a $3 million buyout for 2028.

Teoscar Hernández to the Kansas City Royals

The Dodgers' potential motivations to move Teoscar Hernández stretch beyond just offloading his remaining money, which includes a $14.5 million salary in 2027 and a $6.5 million buyout on a 2028 club option.

With Kyle Tucker and Andy Pages locked into two spots in the outfield and Shohei Ohtani handling everyday designated hitter duties, trading Hernández is the most logical way to create a path for rising star Josue De Paula.

The 21-year-old hit .323/.500/.581 in 42 plate appearances as a September call-up, playing his way onto the postseason roster, and he checked in at No. 3 on the latest B/R Top 100 prospects update.

With a 108 OPS+ and 16 home runs in 125 games, Hernández still provided some legitimate offensive value last season, and the Royals have a clear need for an upgrade in left field.

The return here doesn't rise to the level of a blockbuster deal, but Steven Zobac could serve as rotation depth or a multi-inning arm out of the bullpen where his fastball-slider pairing would potentially play up.

To ATH: LHP Carlos Rodón, $20 million To NYY: IF Zack Gelof

Let's start by clarifying that the only motivation for the Yankees to trade Carlos Rodón would be a legitimate need to shed payroll, so don't expect him to hit the trade block this offseason under normal circumstances.

The 33-year-old got off to a rocky start in pinstripes in 2023, but over the last three seasons he has a 3.35 ERA, 1.12 WHIP and 489 strikeouts in 454.2 innings, and that includes a 2.67 ERA over 16 starts in 2026.

He has two years remaining on his six-year, $162 million deal, which means he would give the Athletics the proven veteran ace they are lacking without representing a massive long-term commitment. The Yankees including some cash might be necessary to maximize their return, and contributing $10 million each in 2027 and 2028 would still represent a solid salary dump.

His recent production means it will take a legitimate return to acquire him, even with his hefty salary, and Zack Gelof could be a great fit to address the Yankees' needs on the infield.

The 27-year-old is controllable through 2029, and while his production has been inconsistent over four seasons in the majors, he had a 116 OPS+ with 22 home runs and 16 steals in a 3.5-WAR season in 2026. He can play second base, third base and all three outfield spots.

articles.title: 30-year-old pitcher Tarik Skubal reportedly made the biggest deal of his career with a staggering $450 million for 9 years
articles.summary: Tarik Skubal has a new home and a new record.
articles.body: Tarik Skubal has a new home and a new record. The two-time Cy Young Award winner agreed to a nine-year, $450 million contract with the New York Mets on Sunday, according to multiple sources. The deal has a full no-trade clause and no opt-outs. The club has not confirmed it because a physical is pending. At $50 million a year, the contract becomes the richest ever for a pitcher, surpassing Yoshinobu Yamamoto's $325 million deal with the Dodgers. The Mets finished last in the NL East, and they went after the biggest arm on the market to fix it.How is Tarik Skubal's $450 million contract structured?Tarik Skubal gets a $45 million signing bonus, and it is shielded from the lockout that threatens the 2027 season (via AP). Another $30 million is deferred and will be paid from 2036 to 2045. The $50 million average tops the old pitcher high of $43.33 million, shared by Max Scherzer and Justin Verlander. Among all players, only Juan Soto ($765 million), Shohei Ohtani ($700 million) and Vladimir Guerrero Jr. ($500 million) have bigger totals.The $450 million left-hander turned 30 on Nov. 20. Over the past four seasons, he is 43-17 with a 2.42 ERA, striking out 655 batters and walking 95 in 546 innings. This year he went 12-7 with a 2.72 ERA in 26 starts for Detroit and Los Angeles, and he missed about six weeks after elbow surgery.Not everyone calls it a bargain. Los Angeles Times columnist Mirjam Swanson pointed to the length. "Skubal's is for the really long haul," she wrote, adding that he has had three elbow surgeries and will collect $50 million every season until he is 39.Mets get an ace, Dodgers step aside, lockout loomsNew York needed help. The Mets went 74-88 even with baseball's biggest opening-day payroll, about $352 million, and their starters posted a 4.47 ERA, 23rd in the majors. Skubal now leads a group that includes Nolan McLean, Christian Scott, Sean Manaea and Kodai Senga.Los Angeles never made an offer, ESPN's Alden Gonzalez reported. The Dodgers wanted him back and were willing to go long-term, but doubts over the new labor deal stopped them before a lockout. Skubal went 1-1 with a 2.45 ERA in two playoff starts for them before Milwaukee swept the NLCS.The signing lands about a week before owners are expected to lock out players. MLB has proposed a hard cap of $258.2 million for 2028, and Skubal and Soto alone would take nearly 40 per cent of it. articles.title: Tarik Skubal's Mets Contract Is What MLB is 'Trying to Eradicate' with Salary Cap, Says Insider
articles.summary: Starting pitcher Tarik Skubal's record-breaking contract with the New York Mets is reportedly the latest example of why MLB owners are looking to implement a salary cap system in the next collective bargaining agreement.
articles.body:
Starting pitcher Tarik Skubal's record-breaking contract with the New York Mets is reportedly the latest example of why MLB owners are looking to implement a salary cap system in the next collective bargaining agreement.

The Athletic's Ken Rosenthal explained that Skubal's nine-year, $450 million contract with the Mets "is the type of deal Major League Baseball is specifically trying to eradicate in its quest for a cap, which almost certainly will lead to a lockout when the collective bargaining agreement expires at 11:59 ET on Dec. 1."

Skubal is now the highest-paid pitcher in MLB history, both by total contract value and average annual value ($50 million). The two-time AL Cy Young Award winner was traded from the Detroit Tigers to the Los Angeles Dodgers last season, adding fuel to the ongoing debate over small-market teams competing against super-powered franchises.

According to Rosenthal, the owners' latest proposal would establish contract maximums of five years, $212 million for a player changing teams and six years, $277 million for a player who stays with the same club.

"Skubal is getting more than twice the first number, and he also had the freedom to go any team he wanted. Under a cap-and-floor system, that freedom would not necessarily exist," Rosenthal explained. "Players would be at the mercy of whichever teams have available cap space."

Skubal's astronomical contract is the type of deal that small-market teams had no chance of matching. Rosenthal noted that the Mets "were one of only a handful of teams with the resources to sign Skubal — and in this free-agent cycle, the only one willing to go as far as they did."

The Toronto Blue Jays and San Diego Padres were also in the mix for Skubal, with the Blue Jays reportedly making "a nine-year offer for slightly more than $400 million." The Padres' offer "is not known," and they were considered "a longshot for Skubal from the start" because of their "existing financial commitments and need for multiple starting pitchers."

In the end, that left the Mets virtually competing against themselves to land the top free-agent pitcher on the market. It remains to be seen if Skubal's arrival will help turn things around for a New York team that missed the playoffs in the last two seasons.

"So, it was [Steve] Cohen. It had to be Cohen," Rosenthal stated. "And the retort to those who think owners like him must be stopped is that the more Cohen spends, the worse his teams seem to get."

articles.title: Red Sox News & Links: Sox weren’t in running for Tarik Skubal, but the top of the rotation didn’t really need him
articles.summary: How good can Payton Tolle get, and how quickly will he get there? These are the questions baseball fans dream on during the long, cold peanuts-and-crackerjac...
articles.body:
How good can Payton Tolle get, and how quickly will he get there? These are the questions baseball fans dream on during the long, cold peanuts-and-crackerjacks-less winters. And in Tolle's case it's easy to dream because, had he pitched a full season, he might have been a Cy Young candidate as a rookie. "[T]he enticing thing is Tolle could be even better based on some of the underlying numbers. Tolle's 3.04 FIP was a near match for his 3.03 ERA, but his 2.70 expected ERA, based on a pitcher's quality and quantity of contact, was a good deal below that mark. That 2.70 xERA placed him in the 95th percentile of all MLB pitchers and only trailed Misiorowski and Max Fried among qualifying pitchers." (Brent Maguire, MLB.com)

Tolle, Garrett Crochet, and Ranger Suarez make up one hell of a top-three, and Jake Bennett showed he can be an effective middle of the rotation starter last season. But, right now, the fifth slot looks a little shaky, with the mercurial Brayan Bello and the extensively injured Tanner Houck and Kutter Crawford battling it out. "Does anyone feel confident about that trio?" asks one writer. "If each pitches to his potential, the Red Sox would be in good position. But both Houck and (especially) Crawford have significant question marks attached because of health, and Bello's performance can hardly be assumed." (Sean McAdam, MassLive)

The Sox aren't done shopping, though. They were amongst the teams interested in Luis Gil, who was a free agent after being non-tendered by the Yankees and subsequently signed with the Detroit Tigers. (Patrick McAvoy, SI.com)

And if you're wondering whether there's another Tolle, Bennett, or Connelly Early down on the farm who could jump into the pitching depth discussion next season, eh, there really isn't. Of the Sox' top 10 prospects according to Alex Speier, #10 John Holobetz is the only pitcher who has even stepped on AA mound. (Alex Speier, Boston Globe)

With such a strong top of the rotation, it's not surprising that the Red Sox didn't even consider going after Tarik Skubal, who signed with the Mets yesterday for more money than has ever before been given to a pitcher. And if the Sox weren't going to get him, at least he didn't end up inside the division. He nearly did, though, as it was the Blue Jays who came in second place for his services. (Daniel Mader, NESN)

Now the Blue Jays will have to look elsewhere to try to rebound from a disappointing season. Here's a look at what the Jays and all the other AL East teams have been doing in the offseason so far. (Peter Abraham, Boston Globe)

articles.title: Padres non-tender JP Sears, Garrett Hawkins
articles.summary: Offseason Notes for November 23
articles.body:
After allowing 34 of their 36 minor league players to go unprotected should there be a Rule 5 Draft, including RHP Francis Peña, No. 19 prospect OF Braedon Karpathios, and No. 27 prospect C Lamar King Jr., the San Diego Padres non-tendered No. 30 prospect Garrett Hawkins after adding him to the 40-man roster last year.

Hawkins failed to sustain his early success as a prospect and ended 2026 with a 5.47 ERA in 54.1 innings with 36 walks to 65 strikeouts over Double-A and Triple-A. Although he was expected to contribute to the Padres' bullpen in 2026, he ultimately struggled with command issues.

LHP JP Sears, acquired from the A's along with Mason Miller in 2025, was never effective for the Padres. During his time in the organization, Sears had a 5.49 ERA in 32.2 innings and spent most of 2026 in Triple-A.

Along with allowing those two pitchers to leave the team, the Padres tendered contracts to closer Mason Miller, catcher Luis Campusano, catcher Freddie Fermin and RHP Jeremiah Estrada.

RHP Bryan Hoeing and RHP Jhony Brito were both signed to deals; no terms were released. Brito, 28, pitched briefly with the Padres in 2026 after completing his injury rehab. He posted a 2.97 ERA in the minors over 69.2 innings of both starting and relieving.

Hoeing lost all of 2026 to flexor tendon surgery.

The MLBPA made a counterproposal to the international draft proposal made by MLB. They rejected the international draft and proposed an increased bonus pool for international signings. They also proposed more oversight to stop teams from engaging in illegal negotiations with underage players. There are proposed fines, suspensions, and other penalties.

MLB rescinded its proposal for eliminating high schoolers from the amateur draft as well as requiring draftees to be at least 20 years old.

With the release of players, free agency, the addition of three pitchers and the non-tendered players, the Padres have 33 players on the 40-man roster.

1B/3B Luis Suisbel, 23, was signed to a minor league contract. A former Seattle Mariners prospect, Suisbel, a switch-hitter, finished 2026 in Double-A and has 42 homers over the past two seasons.

RHP Angel Hernandez, 22, signed a minor league deal after posting a 2.89 ERA in eight games in the Mexican Winter League. He has been assigned to the ACL Padres and is still pitching in Mexico. Originally a Miami Marlins prospect, Hernandez was released in 2024 and played the last two seasons in Mexico.

IF Jose Devers, 23, signed a minor league contract after leaving the Cleveland Guardians minor league system. Signed in 2021, Devers finished 2026 at the Double-A level and hit .270/.348/.345 while playing SS/2B/3B. He is rated as having plus-speed, average defense, but with a subpar hitting tool.

Baseball America released its top 10 prospect list for the Padres. The list is still headed by Ethan Salas until he is no longer eligible. No. 2 RHP Coleman Borthwick, No. 3 IF Elliot Lascelles, No. 4 LHP Kruz Schoolcraft, No. 5 RHP Lan-Hong Su, No. 6 C Ty Harvey, No. 7 OF Ryan Wideman, No. 8 RHP Ryan Lynch, No. 9 RHP Tucker Musgrove, No. 10 RHP Kannon Kemp.

Padres' principal owners, José E. Feliciano and Kwanza Jones, have reportedly offered to purchase the WNBA Los Angeles Sparks from Dodgers owner Mark Walter for $750 million. Walter is selling off many of his sports investments after reports surfaced of a federal insurance fraud investigation.
